newsitem.title: USA: FedEx considers offering Internet discounts.
newsitem.headline: FedEx considers offering Internet discounts.

text.p: Federal Express Corp may consider offering discounts on services purchased through its site on the Internet's World Wide Web, an executive with the company said on Tuesday.

Paul King, senior Federal Express marketing specialist, told the Internet Commerce Expo here that his company was now shipping thousands of packages daily through the Website and that it would soon begin using the facility to collect better market data on customers.
King was asked if Federal Express might promote Internet transactions by offering discounts for online purchases.
"It's certainly been discussed. I would like to have that flexibility to stimulate useage of online applications. But at this point, we don't have firm plans to do that," he replied.

Federal Express' goal would be to offer all of its services and features through the Internet, according to King. He declined to discuss when online operations would reach that point but said he hoped it would be within the next three years.
King said much of the shipments carried out through the Federal Express Website's "ship" application represented new business for the Memphis-based parcel delivery company.
"Much of it's incremental. It's business we would not have gotten if we didn't have that application out there," he said, adding that new business wrung from the Internet presented a double benefit.
"Each order we take for shipping costs us less and each new account we open costs us much less," the Federal Express marketing executive added.

The Federal Express Website, which began in 1994, is now accessed over two million times a month. It is also used to track more than 200,000 packages monthly, and over 150,000 copies of software have been downloaded through the site.

The Website, which Federal Express uses as a 24-hour, seven-day-a-week customer service center, provides the company with a return on investment that has led to what King called "a strict ROI approach to prioritization" in online strategy.
"We have more projects that we can do than we have personnel. So, we're looking for the highest ROI," he said.

"What we're doing (now) is we're looking at ways to where we can provide such added-value information that people will be willing to tell us a little bit about themselves," he said, noting that 65 percent of the company's customer base was interacting electronically when the Website service began.

Meanwhile, he said Federal Express has begun offering a completely integrated online catalogue solution for business customers, called Fedex Virtual Order. The solution partly represents a means for leveraging the Fedex brand name.
"A company can give us their goods. We warehouse them, set them up on the Web. They never even see the product," King explained.

"We view it as risk-sharing through the variable cost. If we put a customer on line and they don't sell many goods, we don't really gain (and) they don't really lose. So, we're looking to share some risk with these people."
